triage.name: Meconium aspiration syndrome
triage.reason: Infant born through meconium-stained fluid with respiratory distress and patchy infiltrates; diagnosis made from delivery history, exam, blood gas and imaging.

demographics: Occurs in newborns; incidence is higher in post-term and small-for-gestational-age infants
More common in pregnancies complicated by fetal distress or meconium-stained amniotic fluid

risk_factors.text: Fetal distress or non-reassuring fetal heart tracing during labor
Intrauterine growth restriction or small for gestational age

comorbidities: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn

chief_complaints.text: My baby is having trouble breathing
The baby was born through greenish fluid

hpi.duration: Present from delivery; respiratory distress evident within the first minutes to hours of life
hpi.progression: Respiratory distress develops immediately after delivery and may worsen over the first 24–48 hours as meconium obstructs small airways and causes inflammation
hpi.quality: Labored breathing with grunting, nasal flaring, retractions, and tachypnea
hpi.severity: Moderate to severe; often requires supplemental oxygen and respiratory support
pertinent_negatives: Fever in the mother before delivery
Immediate crying and normal breathing after birth
Congenital heart defect known before delivery

positives.text: Low Apgar scores at 1 and 5 minutes

atypical.how_it_differs: Preterm infants may have milder meconium passage but still develop respiratory distress; meconium aspiration is less common in preterm than term/post-term infants.

general.mild: Alert, vigorous, pink with minimal oxygen requirement; mild tachypnea and grunting
general.moderate: Ill-appearing but responsive, tachypneic with grunting, nasal flaring, and retractions; requires supplemental oxygen
general.severe: Lethargic, dusky, marked respiratory distress with severe retractions and grunting; requires CPAP or mechanical ventilation
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, pale or cyanotic, apneic or gasping, poor perfusion; requires intubation and intensive support

labs.caveat: Acidemia from airway obstruction, atelectasis and persistent pulmonary hypertension; a low pH with a normal PaCO2 suggests a mixed or metabolic component from perinatal asphyxia.
Rises as small airways obstruct and the infant fatigues; a normal or low PaCO2 early does not exclude severe disease.
Hypoxemia is often out of proportion to the chest x-ray because of right-to-left shunting through persistent pulmonary hypertension.
A negative base excess reflects the metabolic component of perinatal asphyxia and helps gauge severity.
Elevated from tissue hypoperfusion and hypoxemia; a high value supports perinatal asphyxia and poor perfusion.
Mild leukocytosis is common after stress or asphyxia and does not by itself prove infection; a normal or low white count does not exclude sepsis.
Hypoglycemia from increased work of breathing and asphyxia; must be checked and corrected promptly in any distressed newborn.
Elevated when perinatal asphyxia causes acute kidney injury; creatinine in the first days of life also reflects the maternal value.
Low bicarbonate reflects metabolic acidosis from asphyxia or hypoperfusion.
Nonspecific in the first hours of life; a normal value does not exclude early-onset sepsis, and serial values are more useful.

findings.finding: Right ventricular dominance with right axis deviation, which is normal in a newborn and should not be mistaken for right ventricular hypertrophy from pulmonary hypertension
Nonspecific ST-T flattening or T-wave changes from hypoxemia and acidosis

findings.text: Patchy, coarse, asymmetric infiltrates or opacities
Hyperinflation with a flattened diaphragm and increased anteroposterior diameter
Pneumothorax or pneumomediastinum from air leak
Normal-appearing lungs early in the course despite significant hypoxemia

Elevated estimated right ventricular or pulmonary artery pressure
Structurally normal heart with no congenital defect

decision_points: Confirm that the infant was born through meconium-stained amniotic fluid and has respiratory distress before attributing the picture to meconium aspiration
Check a blood gas early; hypoxemia out of proportion to the chest x-ray should prompt an echocardiogram for persistent pulmonary hypertension
Treat for early-onset sepsis until cultures are negative when risk factors are present, because the presentation overlaps with pneumonia and sepsis
Watch for air leak (pneumothorax) if the infant deteriorates suddenly

criteria.name: Clinical diagnosis of meconium aspiration syndrome
criteria.summary: Diagnosis is clinical and requires all of: birth through meconium-stained amniotic fluid, early respiratory distress in the newborn, characteristic patchy infiltrates with hyperinflation on chest x-ray, and no alternative explanation for the respiratory distress.

differential.name: Neonatal pneumonia (congenital or early-onset bacterial)
differential.why_considered: A distressed newborn with tachypnea, grunting, hypoxemia and patchy lung opacities looks identical to meconium aspiration; both can follow prolonged rupture of membranes or maternal fever.
differential.trigger: Maternal fever, foul-smelling fluid, prolonged rupture of membranes, or worsening respiratory distress despite respiratory support

history: Prolonged rupture of membranes or maternal fever before delivery
Clear rather than meconium-stained amniotic fluid
Group B streptococcus colonization or prior infant with early-onset sepsis
exam: Ill appearance with poor perfusion out of proportion to lung findings
labs: Elevated or rising CRP on serial measurement
Leukocytosis or leukopenia with left shift
imaging: Lobar or segmental consolidation rather than diffuse coarse patchy infiltrates
Pleural effusion more common than in meconium aspiration

differential.name: Transient tachypnea of the newborn
differential.why_considered: A term or late-preterm infant with early tachypnea and mild hypoxemia after delivery; the most common cause of early neonatal respiratory distress.

history: Cesarean delivery or precipitous delivery without fetal distress
exam: Tachypnea without marked grunting or retractions
Mild oxygen requirement that improves quickly
labs: Mild or no acidosis on blood gas
imaging: Perihilar streaking and fluid in the fissures
Normal or slightly increased lung volumes without coarse infiltrates

differential.name: Respiratory distress syndrome (hyaline membrane disease)
differential.why_considered: A preterm infant with grunting, retractions, hypoxemia and diffuse lung disease shortly after birth.

history: Infant of a diabetic mother or no antenatal corticosteroids
exam: Progressive worsening over the first hours
imaging: Diffuse ground-glass opacities with air bronchograms
Low lung volumes rather than hyperinflation

differential.name: Neonatal sepsis
differential.why_considered: A lethargic, poorly perfused newborn with respiratory distress, temperature instability and acidosis; can coexist with meconium aspiration.
differential.trigger: Temperature instability, hypotension, poor perfusion, or lethargy disproportionate to the respiratory findings

history: Maternal fever, chorioamnionitis, or prolonged rupture of membranes
Risk factors for group B streptococcus
labs: Leukopenia or marked leukocytosis with left shift
imaging: Chest x-ray may be normal or show nonspecific opacities

differential.name: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
differential.why_considered: Severe hypoxemia that is out of proportion to the chest x-ray, often complicating meconium aspiration and other perinatal stress.
differential.trigger: Hypoxemia out of proportion to lung findings, or a difference in preductal and postductal oxygen saturation

history: Perinatal asphyxia, meconium aspiration, or sepsis as a trigger
exam: Single loud second heart sound or tricuspid regurgitation murmur
Difference in preductal and postductal saturations
labs: Severe hypoxemia with relatively preserved PaCO2 early
imaging: Echocardiogram shows right-to-left or bidirectional shunting and elevated pulmonary pressures

differential.name: Congenital heart disease (cyanotic, e.g. transposition of the great arteries)
differential.why_considered: Cyanosis and hypoxemia in a newborn that does not improve with supplemental oxygen.
differential.trigger: Cyanosis with no or minimal respiratory distress, or hypoxemia unresponsive to oxygen

history: Antenatal suspicion or family history of congenital heart disease
exam: Murmur, single second heart sound, or abnormal pulses
Cyanosis with clear lungs and minimal retractions
imaging: Chest x-ray may show abnormal cardiac silhouette or pulmonary vascularity

differential.name: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia
differential.why_considered: A newborn with severe respiratory distress, cyanosis and a scaphoid abdomen shortly after birth.
differential.trigger: Scaphoid abdomen with bowel sounds in the chest and severe distress at birth

exam: Bowel sounds heard in the chest
imaging: Chest x-ray shows bowel loops in the hemithorax with mediastinal shift
Nasogastric tube coiled in the chest

differential.name: Pneumothorax
differential.why_considered: Sudden deterioration with hypoxemia and respiratory distress in a ventilated or spontaneously breathing newborn; a known complication of meconium aspiration.
differential.trigger: Abrupt worsening of respiratory status or asymmetric breath sounds

history: Sudden deterioration rather than gradual onset
exam: Hyperresonance and shifted apical impulse on the affected side
labs: Acute rise in PaCO2 and fall in PaO2
imaging: Chest x-ray shows a visible pleural line with absent lung markings peripherally

severity.mild: Term infant with tachypnea and mild grunting, oxygen requirement below 40%, normal or near-normal blood gas, and patchy infiltrates on chest x-ray; feeding may be briefly withheld.
severity.moderate: Marked distress with grunting, retractions and nasal flaring, oxygen requirement 40–70%, respiratory acidosis on blood gas, and coarse infiltrates with hyperinflation; needs CPAP or high-flow support and NICU care.
severity.severe: Severe distress with cyanosis, oxygen requirement above 70% or FiO2 near 1.0, significant hypoxemia and hypercapnia, and evidence of persistent pulmonary hypertension; requires mechanical ventilation and often inhaled nitric oxide.
severity.critical: Respiratory failure with refractory hypoxemia, severe acidosis, hemodynamic instability, air leak, or need for extracorporeal membrane oxygenation; high risk of death without escalation of intensive care.

red_flags.finding: Hypoxemia out of proportion to the chest x-ray or a difference in preductal and postductal oxygen saturation
red_flags.meaning: Suggests persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn with right-to-left shunting; needs echocardiography and pulmonary vasodilator therapy

red_flags.finding: Sudden deterioration with asymmetric breath sounds or a shift in the apical impulse
red_flags.meaning: Pneumothorax or pneumomediastinum; requires immediate needle decompression or chest tube

red_flags.finding: Apnea, gasping, or a falling respiratory rate in a previously tachypneic infant
red_flags.meaning: Impending respiratory failure from fatigue; requires immediate intubation and ventilation

red_flags.finding: Hypotension, prolonged capillary refill, or mottling
red_flags.meaning: Shock from asphyxia, sepsis, or air leak; needs fluid resuscitation, vasopressors, and a sepsis evaluation

red_flags.finding: Severe metabolic acidosis with elevated lactate
red_flags.meaning: Perinatal asphyxia or poor perfusion; predicts multiorgan injury and worse outcome
Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy or hypoglycemia; requires glucose check, neurologic evaluation, and possible therapeutic hypothermia

complications.name: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
clues: Hypoxemia out of proportion to lung findings
Difference in preductal and postductal saturations

complications.name: Chronic lung disease or reactive airway symptoms
clues: Persistent oxygen requirement beyond the neonatal period
Abnormal pulmonary function testing later in childhood

complications.name: Feeding difficulties and gastroesophageal reflux
clues: Need for thickened feeds or reflux medication

special_populations.differences: Preterm infants are less likely to pass meconium before birth but can still develop meconium aspiration; they are more prone to respiratory distress syndrome and air leak, and their immature lungs tolerate hypoxemia poorly.

Maternal factors such as preeclampsia, hypertension, diabetes, and post-term gestation increase the risk of meconium-stained fluid and fetal distress; delivery room management focuses on preventing aspiration and supporting the newborn.

key_questions.question: What color was the amniotic fluid when your baby was born?
key_questions.looking_for: Meconium-stained (green, brown, or thick 'pea soup') fluid; the key exposure for meconium aspiration

key_questions.question: How far along was the pregnancy at delivery?
key_questions.looking_for: Post-term (beyond 41 weeks) or term gestation; post-term infants are at highest risk

key_questions.question: When did the breathing trouble start — right at birth or later?
key_questions.looking_for: Distress within the first minutes to hours of life; later onset suggests other causes

key_questions.question: Was there any fetal distress or an abnormal heart tracing during labor?
key_questions.looking_for: Non-reassuring fetal heart tracing, fetal bradycardia, or need for resuscitation, suggesting perinatal asphyxia

key_questions.question: Did the baby cry and breathe normally right after delivery?
key_questions.looking_for: Depressed cry or poor respiratory effort at birth; a vigorous immediate cry argues against significant aspiration

key_questions.question: How was the baby delivered, and was there a difficult or prolonged labor?
key_questions.looking_for: Difficult or prolonged labor, instrumental delivery, or emergency cesarean for fetal distress

key_questions.question: How much oxygen or breathing support has the baby needed since birth?
key_questions.looking_for: Escalating oxygen requirement or need for CPAP/ventilation, indicating severity

key_questions.question: Has the baby been feeding, and is the baby alert and responsive?
key_questions.looking_for: Poor feeding, lethargy, or decreased responsiveness suggesting asphyxia or sepsis

key_questions.question: Did the mother have a fever, foul-smelling fluid, or prolonged rupture of membranes before delivery?
key_questions.looking_for: Risk factors for congenital or early-onset bacterial pneumonia/sepsis, which can mimic this picture

key_questions.question: Was the baby born early (preterm)?
key_questions.looking_for: Preterm gestation, which points more toward respiratory distress syndrome than meconium aspiration

key_questions.question: Is there any family history of cystic fibrosis or congenital heart disease?
key_questions.looking_for: Alternative explanations for neonatal respiratory distress

key_questions.question: Has the baby had any seizures, or has the baby's color or breathing suddenly worsened?
key_questions.looking_for: Seizures (hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy) or abrupt deterioration (pneumothorax) requiring immediate action

reasoning_points: Birth through meconium-stained amniotic fluid, often with fetal distress or post-term gestation
Early respiratory distress in the newborn: tachypnea, grunting, nasal flaring, retractions, and cyanosis
Hypoxemia on blood gas, sometimes out of proportion to the chest x-ray because of persistent pulmonary hypertension
Chest x-ray showing patchy coarse infiltrates with hyperinflation and flattened diaphragms
Meconium staining of the skin, nails, and umbilical cord supporting the exposure
No alternative explanation such as congenital heart disease, sepsis, or respiratory distress syndrome
Recognition of complications: persistent pulmonary hypertension, air leak, and hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy

easy: Term or post-term infant born through thick meconium-stained fluid
Immediate respiratory distress with grunting, retractions, and cyanosis
Meconium staining of skin, nails, and umbilical cord
Chest x-ray with patchy infiltrates and hyperinflation
medium: Mild tachypnea with only a modest oxygen requirement and a nearly normal chest x-ray early on
Overlap with transient tachypnea of the newborn or early-onset pneumonia
Hypoxemia out of proportion to lung findings suggesting persistent pulmonary hypertension
Preterm infant with meconium-stained fluid but a picture that could also be respiratory distress syndrome
hard: Sudden deterioration from a pneumothorax complicating the course
Cyanotic congenital heart disease presenting with hypoxemia unresponsive to oxygen
Congenital diaphragmatic hernia with a scaphoid abdomen and bowel sounds in the chest
Concurrent early-onset sepsis with temperature instability and poor perfusion
Seizures or marked lethargy from hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy obscuring the respiratory picture
